h1: Big brewery or craft brewery: where to start your brewing career
title: Big Brewery or Craft Brewery First? | Craft Beer School
desc: Should you start your brewing career at a large brewery or a craft brewery? The trade-offs in learning, structure, skills and progression in India.
teaser: At a large brewery you might spend a year learning one section properly. At a brewpub you might do every job in your first week.
standfirst: New brewers often ask whether to start at a large brewery or a craft brewery. Both build real skills, in different ways. We compare what you learn, how you work and where each path tends to lead in India.
sections: Two very different places to learn

A large brewery produces huge volumes of a few beers with high consistency. It runs on systems, specialist teams, automation and strict procedures. A craft brewery or brewpub makes smaller batches of many beers, often by hand, with a small team doing a bit of everything.

Both are good places to learn brewing. They teach different things. The right choice depends on your goals, your background and what you enjoy. Our guide to brewpubs and microbreweries explains the craft side in more detail.

• Process discipline. Standard operating procedures, checks, records and why each step matters.
  • Quality systems. Labs, specifications, statistical control and audits.
  • Scale. Large brewhouses, automated control systems, high-speed packaging lines, centrifuges and filters.
  • Safety culture. Permits, lock-out procedures and formal training.
  • Specialisation. You may focus on one area, (brewhouse, fermentation, packaging or quality) and learn it deeply.

The trade-off is that you may not brew a recipe of your own for years. Roles can be narrow. You may spend long periods on one section or shift pattern. Entry is often through graduate or trainee programmes, with competition for places.

• Breadth. Milling, mashing, boiling, fermenting, cellaring, cleaning, kegging and sometimes serving, all in your first months.
  • Hands-on skills. Manual valves, hoses, tank cleaning and problem solving without a large support team.
  • Recipe exposure. Brewing many styles and seeing recipe development up close.
  • Business awareness. Seeing costs, sales and customers directly.
  • Responsibility. Small teams give you real responsibility quickly.

The trade-offs are less formal training, fewer systems and sometimes less consistent quality practice. Hours can be long and physical. Progression depends on the brewery's growth. Quality varies a lot between craft breweries, so the brewery you pick matters as much as the type.

If you have a degree in chemical engineering, microbiology, food technology or biotechnology, a large brewery trainee programme can use your training well and give you a structured start. If you are a homebrewer or career changer without a technical degree, a craft brewery or brewpub is often more accessible, starting as a cellar hand or assistant brewer.

Think about what you enjoy. If you like systems, data and mastering a process, large breweries suit you. If you like variety, creativity and doing things with your hands, craft brewing may fit better. Our guide to cellar and packaging jobs covers common first roles in both.

Many brewers work in both during their careers. A few years at a large brewery gives you process and quality discipline that craft breweries value highly. Brewers who move to craft with that background often bring better cleaning, measurement and consistency practices.

Brewpubs whose head brewer trained in a large plant often show it in tidier records and stricter cleaning habits. It is not a rule, but the habits travel.

Craft experience has its own value in a large plant. A brewer who has run a whole brew day alone understands how each stage affects the next, which helps when troubleshooting across departments.

Moving from craft to large brewing is possible too, especially for brewers with strong technical knowledge and quality experience. It can be harder without formal qualifications, because large brewers often hire through structured programmes.

Whichever type you consider, ask:

  • Who will train me? How?
  • What tasks will I do in my first three months?
  • How does the brewery check quality? Is there a lab, logs or tasting panel?
  • What safety training is provided?
  • Where have people in this role moved on to?

The answers tell you more about your learning than the brewery's size. A well-run small brewery can teach more than a badly run large one. The reverse is also true.

Whichever path you choose, understanding brewing science helps you learn faster and make a better impression. Knowing why mash temperature affects body, how yeast behaves and what causes off flavours lets you ask better questions on day one. It also helps you judge a brewery during the interview, because you can tell whether its answers about quality make sense. Our guide to jobs in a brewery shows how roles connect across both types.
faqs: Is it better to start at a big brewery or a craft brewery?
Both build real skills. Large breweries teach process discipline and specialisation, while craft breweries teach breadth and hands-on brewing. Choose based on your background and goals.
Can I join a large brewery without a technical degree?
It is harder, because large brewers often hire through trainee programmes for graduates. Craft breweries are often more accessible for career changers.
Can brewers move from craft to large breweries later?
Yes, especially with strong technical knowledge and quality experience, though structured hiring at large brewers can make it harder without formal qualifications.
